Generators build graphs from a recipe instead of from data. A few parameters describe a whole
family of graphs: a grid of a given size, a tree of a given depth, or a random network with a given
number of nodes and a given chance of an edge between any two. Generated graphs are the standard
material for testing algorithms, for teaching, for benchmarks, and for null models that tell you
whether a pattern in real data is more than chance.

EdgeCase has nearly a hundred generators. Most of them are `Graph` methods whose names start with
`add_`, because they *add* the generated structure to the graph they are called on. On an empty
graph that simply builds the structure, and on a graph that already has nodes, it adds a new
component beside them.

## The common pattern

Calling a generator on an empty `Graph` is the usual way to start:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec

grid = ec.Graph().add_grid_2d(rows=3, cols=4)
grid
```

The deterministic generators share three optional arguments:

- `type=` sets the `type` of every new node,
- `rel=` sets the `rel` of every new edge, and
- `label=` controls labels. By default each new node is labelled with its ID as a string (`"1"`,
  `"2"`, and so on), or with a label that describes its position when the structure has a natural
  one. `label=False` leaves the nodes unlabelled.

The grid's nodes are labelled by their row and column:

```{python}
grid.get_node_df().head(5)
```

Because generators add to an existing graph, several can be combined in one graph. Here two cycles
of different types sit side by side in one graph, each as its own component. Their labels are
their IDs, so the two sets of labels don't collide:

```{python}
rings = (
    ec.Graph()
    .add_cycle_graph(n=4, type="small", rel="ring")
    .add_cycle_graph(n=6, type="large", rel="ring")
)
rings.count_weakly_connected_components(), rings.get_node_df()["label"].to_list()
```

The graph has two components, and the six-node cycle's labels continue from 5, where the first
cycle's left off.

## Deterministic structures

These generators always produce the same graph for the same arguments.

| Family | Methods |
|---|---|
| Paths, cycles, stars, wheels | `add_path_graph()`, `add_cycle_graph()`, `add_star_graph()`, `add_wheel_graph()` |
| Complete graphs | `add_full_graph()`, `add_complete_bipartite_graph()`, `add_complete_multipartite_graph()`, `add_turan_graph()` |
| Trees | `add_balanced_tree()`, `add_binomial_tree()`, `add_full_rary_tree()` |
| Lattices | `add_grid_2d()`, `add_grid_graph()` (any dimension, optionally periodic), `add_triangular_lattice_graph()`, `add_hexagonal_lattice_graph()`, `add_hypercube_graph()` |
| Composite shapes | `add_barbell_graph()`, `add_lollipop_graph()`, `add_tadpole_graph()`, `add_windmill_graph()`, `add_ladder_graph()`, `add_prism_graph()` |
| Algebraic families | `add_circulant_graph()`, `add_kneser_graph()`, `add_johnson_graph()`, `add_generalized_petersen_graph()`, `add_lcf_graph()`, `add_mycielski_graph()` |
| Expanders | `add_margulis_gabber_galil_graph()`, `add_chordal_cycle_graph()`, `add_paley_graph()` |
| Puzzles | `add_sudoku_graph()` |

A balanced tree, for example, takes a branching factor `k` and a height `h`:

```{python}
tree = ec.Graph().add_balanced_tree(k=2, h=3)
tree.count_nodes(), tree.is_tree()
```

The barbell graph, two complete graphs joined by a path, is a classic stress test for algorithms
that rely on short paths: random walks get trapped in one bell or the other, and the nodes on the
bar have high betweenness despite their low degree:

```{python}
ec.Graph().add_barbell_graph(m1=5, m2=3).plot(size_by="degree", seed=2, width=500, height=300)
```

Generators for bipartite and multipartite graphs record which part each node belongs to in a node
attribute, `part` by default (change it with `part_attr=`):

```{python}
k34 = ec.Graph().add_complete_bipartite_graph(n1=3, n2=4)
k34.get_node_df()
```

### Named graphs

[`add_named_graph()`](../reference/Graph.add_named_graph.qmd) adds one of about thirty graphs that
are famous enough to have names: the Platonic solids, the small cages, and standard examples and
counterexamples. The Petersen graph is the most famous of all, a 3-regular graph on ten nodes that
is a counterexample to many plausible-sounding conjectures:

```{python}
petersen = ec.Graph().add_named_graph("petersen")
petersen.is_regular(), petersen.get_girth(), petersen.chromatic_number_upper_bound()
```

It is regular, its shortest cycle has length 5, and a greedy coloring colors it with three colors
(which is optimal, since its 5-cycles rule out two). The Krackhardt kite is
another useful one: a ten-node network built so that degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality
each pick out a different most central node.

```{python}
ec.Graph().add_named_graph("krackhardt kite").plot(label_by="id", node_size=12, seed=4)
```

Names ignore case, and spaces or hyphens can stand in for underscores. The reference page lists
every available name.

### Every small graph

Two methods enumerate graphs rather than build one. `atlas_graphs()` returns all 1,253 graphs on
up to seven nodes from *An Atlas of Graphs*, in the book's order, and `add_atlas_graph()` adds
one of them by index. `iter_nonisomorphic_trees()` yields every distinct tree with a given number
of nodes, which is handy for testing an algorithm exhaustively on small inputs:

```{python}
trees = list(ec.Graph().iter_nonisomorphic_trees(order=6))
len(trees), [max(t.degrees(return_dict=True).values()) for t in trees]
```

There are six trees on six nodes, from the path (maximum degree 2) to the star (maximum degree 5).

## Random graphs

Random generators take a `seed=` argument. With a seed, the same call gives the same graph every
time, which is what you want in tests, documentation, and any analysis that needs to be
reproducible. Without one, each call gives a different graph.

```{python}
a = ec.Graph().add_gnp_graph(n=30, p=0.1, seed=11)
b = ec.Graph().add_gnp_graph(n=30, p=0.1, seed=11)
a.get_edges_as_tuples() == b.get_edges_as_tuples()
```

Some of the older random generators (`add_gnp_graph()`, `add_gnm_graph()`, `add_pa_graph()`, and
`add_smallworld_graph()`) leave their nodes unlabelled, so refer to their nodes by ID.

### The classic models

Each classic model explains a different feature of real networks:

| Model | Method | What it produces |
|---|---|---|
| Erdős–Rényi G(n, p) | `add_gnp_graph()` | every possible edge present independently with probability `p` |
| Erdős–Rényi G(n, m) | `add_gnm_graph()` | exactly `m` edges, placed uniformly at random |
| Watts–Strogatz | `add_smallworld_graph()`, `add_newman_watts_strogatz_graph()`, `add_connected_watts_strogatz_graph()` | high clustering together with short paths (small worlds) |
| Barabási–Albert | `add_pa_graph()`, `add_extended_barabasi_albert_graph()`, `add_dual_barabasi_albert_graph()` | a heavy-tailed degree distribution with a few large hubs (scale-free networks) |
| Holme–Kim | `add_powerlaw_cluster_graph()` | hubs *and* high clustering |
| Random regular | `add_random_regular_graph()` | every node with the same degree, otherwise random |
| Random trees | `add_random_labeled_tree()`, `add_random_powerlaw_tree()`, `add_random_lobster()` | trees drawn at random |

The difference between the models shows up clearly in their degree distributions. A preferential
attachment graph grows by adding nodes that link preferentially to nodes that already have many
links, which produces hubs far larger than anything an Erdős–Rényi graph of the same size and
density would contain:

```{python}
pa = ec.Graph().add_pa_graph(n=500, m=2, seed=1)
er = ec.Graph().add_gnm_graph(n=500, m=pa.count_edges(), seed=1)

max(pa.degrees(return_dict=True).values()), max(er.degrees(return_dict=True).values())
```

Both graphs have 500 nodes and the same number of edges, but the largest hub of the preferential
attachment graph has more than five times the degree of the busiest node in the random graph.

A small-world graph starts as a ring in which each node is linked to its `k` nearest neighbors, and
then rewires each edge with probability `p`. Even a little rewiring shortens paths dramatically
while leaving most of the local clustering intact:

```{python}
for p in [0.0, 0.05, 0.5]:
    sw = ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=200, k=6, p=p, seed=3)
    print(f"p={p:<4}  clustering={sw.get_transitivity():.3f}  mean distance={sw.get_mean_distance():.2f}")
```

Rewiring 5% of the edges cuts the mean distance between nodes by more than two thirds, while the
clustering barely changes. Rewiring half of them leaves a graph that is close to random, with short
paths but little clustering.

### Degree sequences

Sometimes the degree of every node is known and everything else should be random. These
generators realize a given degree sequence:

- `configuration_model()` pairs up edge "stubs" at random. It can produce self-loops and parallel
  edges, and it returns a new graph, with nodes labelled `"0"`, `"1"`, and so on.
- `add_havel_hakimi_graph()` builds a simple graph deterministically, and
  `add_random_degree_sequence_graph()` a simple graph at random.
- `add_directed_configuration_model()` and `add_directed_havel_hakimi_graph()` take separate in-
  and out-degree sequences.
- `add_joint_degree_graph()` matches the number of edges between nodes of each pair of degrees,
  and `expected_degree_graph()` matches degrees on average (the Chung–Lu model).

```{python}
sequence = [4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1]
hh = ec.Graph().add_havel_hakimi_graph(sequence)
sorted(hh.degrees(return_dict=True).values(), reverse=True)
```

### Null models from an existing graph

A common question about a real network is whether some feature of it, such as its clustering or
its number of triangles, is more than its degree sequence alone would produce.
[`random_reference()`](../reference/Graph.random_reference.qmd) answers it by returning a
randomized copy of a graph in which every node keeps its degree but the wiring is shuffled, by
repeatedly swapping the endpoints of pairs of edges. Comparing the original with a few randomized
copies gives the baseline:

```{python}
dolphins = ec.dolphins()
shuffled = [dolphins.random_reference(niter=10, seed=s).get_transitivity() for s in range(5)]

round(dolphins.get_transitivity(), 3), [round(t, 3) for t in shuffled]
```

The dolphins' transitivity (the fraction of connected triples that close into triangles) is more
than double that of the randomized copies, so their associations close into triangles far more
often than their degrees alone would explain. The `niter=` argument sets how many times, on
average, each edge is rewired. By default `random_reference()` keeps the graph connected;
[`degree_preserving_rewire()`](../reference/Graph.degree_preserving_rewire.qmd) performs a set
number of swaps, `n_swaps=`, without that restriction.
[Clustering and motifs](15-clustering-and-motifs.qmd#motifs) uses these randomizations to test the
significance of triangles and other small patterns.

### Spatial and growth models

Some models place nodes in space and connect the nearby ones. `add_random_geometric_graph()` joins
nodes within a given radius, and `add_waxman_graph()`, `add_soft_random_geometric_graph()`,
`add_geographical_threshold_graph()`, and `add_navigable_small_world_graph()` are variations on the
idea. Except for `add_random_geometric_graph()`, they store each node's coordinates in a `pos`
attribute, which `plot(layout="pos")` can use to draw the graph in its own space (see
[Layouts](23-layouts.qmd)):

```{python}
waxman = ec.Graph().add_waxman_graph(n=40, beta=0.6, alpha=0.15, seed=5)
waxman.plot(layout="pos", show_labels=False, width=500, height=350)
```

Others grow a network one node at a time. `add_gn_graph()`, `add_gnr_graph()`, and
`add_gnc_graph()` grow directed trees and networks, as citations or web links accumulate;
`add_scale_free_graph()` grows a directed scale-free graph; and `add_duplication_divergence_graph()`
and `add_partial_duplication_graph()` model the growth of protein interaction networks by gene
duplication.

### Bipartite models

`add_bipartite_gnp_graph()`, `add_bipartite_gnm_graph()`, `add_bipartite_configuration_model()`,
`add_bipartite_havel_hakimi_graph()`, and `add_bipartite_preferential_attachment_graph()` build
random two-part graphs, such as people and the events they attend, and store each node's part in the
`part` attribute.

## Community benchmarks

To test a community detection method, you need a graph whose communities are known. The benchmark
generators plant communities and record each node's community in a node attribute, `community` by
default (change it with `community_attr=`):

| Method | Communities |
|---|---|
| `add_caveman_graph()` | disconnected cliques |
| `add_connected_caveman_graph()`, `add_ring_of_cliques()` | cliques joined in a ring |
| `add_relaxed_caveman_graph()` | cliques with a fraction of their edges rewired at random |
| `add_planted_partition_graph()` | equal groups, with edge probabilities `p_in` inside and `p_out` between |
| `add_random_partition_graph()` | groups of given sizes, with `p_in` and `p_out` |
| `add_gaussian_random_partition_graph()` | groups of random, normally distributed sizes |
| `add_lfr_graph()` | the LFR benchmark: power-law degrees and community sizes, with a mixing parameter `mu` |
| `generate_stochastic_block_model()` | any matrix of edge probabilities between groups |

The planted partition model is the simplest of these. Here are four groups of ten nodes, with
edges much more likely inside groups than between them:

```{python}
planted = ec.Graph().add_planted_partition_graph(
    num_groups=4, group_size=10, p_in=0.5, p_out=0.02, seed=8
)
planted.plot(color_by="community", show_labels=False, seed=8, width=500, height=350)
```

With the true communities stored, a detection method can be checked against them. Running Louvain
and cross-tabulating its communities against the planted ones shows how well it recovered them:

```{python}
(
    planted.cmty_louvain()
    .get_node_df()
    .group_by("community", "cmty_louvain")
    .len()
    .sort("community", "cmty_louvain")
)
```

Each planted community maps onto exactly one detected community, so Louvain recovered the planted
structure perfectly. Raising `p_out`, or the mixing parameter `mu` of the LFR benchmark, makes the
communities harder to find. [Community detection](14-communities.qmd) has more on comparing
methods.

## Graphs from data

A few generators turn other kinds of data into graphs:

- `add_visibility_graph()` turns a time series into a graph in which two time points are joined
  when the straight line between them passes above every point in between. The structure of the
  graph reflects the structure of the series: periodic series give regular graphs, and fractal
  series give scale-free ones.
- `add_interval_graph()` joins intervals that overlap.
- `add_prefix_tree()` builds a trie from a list of sequences.

```{python}
series = [3, 1, 2, 5, 1, 4]
visibility = ec.Graph().add_visibility_graph(series)
visibility.get_node_df()
```

The value of each time point is stored in the `value` attribute. The fourth point, the peak of the
series at 5, can see every other point, so it has the highest degree.
